articles.title: Histotripsy for Liver Malignancies: A Systematic Review of the Existing Literature.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 10 clinical studies (2022–2026) finds that histotripsy, a noninvasive nonthermal ablation technique, achieves high technical success and short-term tumor control in liver malignancies but lacks long-term comparative data.
summary: This systematic review synthesized PubMed and Scopus databases through August 2026 (PRISMA-compliant) to evaluate histotripsy—an emerging noninvasive, nonthermal ablative approach—for primary and secondary liver tumors. Ten clinical studies met inclusion criteria, enrolling patients with hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases from colorectal, neuroendocrine, pancreatic, breast, and other cancers.

Technical success ranged from 68.8% to 100%, though outcome definitions varied. Early treatment efficacy and local control rates generally exceeded 90% in successfully treated tumors. Major complications were uncommon; vascular thrombosis and acute kidney injury were identified as potential safety concerns. Longer-term oncologic outcomes remained limited by heterogeneous imaging criteria, treatment intent, and patient population definitions.

The authors conclude that current evidence supports the technical feasibility and short-term efficacy of hepatic histotripsy. However, standardized outcome reporting, extended follow-up periods, and comparative effectiveness studies relative to established liver-directed therapies (resection, transplant, radiofrequency ablation, transarterial chemoembolization) are necessary to determine durability and clinical role.
articles.why: Histotripsy represents a potential addition to the armamentarium of liver-directed therapies, particularly because it is nonthermal and noninvasive. This review may inform multidisciplinary discussions about patient selection and sequencing of ablative approaches, especially in cases where thermal methods are contraindicated or when preservation of liver function is critical. The identified safety signals (vascular events, renal injury) warrant attention in clinical practice pending confirmatory data.
articles.evidence: Systematic review of 10 clinical studies published 2022–2026. No aggregate sample size reported in the abstract. Study populations and treatment intentions were heterogeneous. Major limitations: (1) heterogeneous imaging criteria and outcome definitions across studies; (2) limited long-term follow-up data; (3) no head-to-head randomized comparisons with standard therapies; (4) absence of reported baseline patient characteristics, comorbidity burden, or tumor staging in this abstract. Causality cannot be established for the safety signals noted.

articles.title: Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial.
articles.dek: Empirical tuberculosis treatment did not reduce mortality in HIV-infected infants hospitalized with severe pneumonia compared with a strategy guided by clinical findings and microbiological testing.
summary: EMPIRICAL was a multicentre, open-label, randomized controlled trial across six African countries enrolling 558 infants aged 28–365 days with severe HIV-associated pneumonia. Participants were assigned to receive standard of care (antibiotics, cotrimoxazole, and steroids) with or without 6 months of tuberculosis treatment and/or 15 days of valganciclovir. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 15 days and 360 days.

At 12 months, mortality was 48% (132 of 276) in the empirical tuberculosis treatment groups and 43% (121 of 282) in the non-empirical groups (adjusted hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.87–1.43; p=0.3868). There was no difference at 15 days or in serious adverse events. Notably, 46% of participants in the non-empirical groups eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up, with 20% confirmed by microbiological testing and 27% based on clinical suspicion.

The findings do not support empirical tuberculosis treatment as superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided approach for this population. However, the substantial crossover to tuberculosis treatment in the comparison group may have reduced the contrast between strategies, potentially limiting the ability to detect a treatment effect if one exists.
articles.why: This trial addresses a clinically important question in regions with high tuberculosis and HIV burden: whether treating tuberculosis presumptively in severely ill infants saves lives when microbiological confirmation is pending. The lack of mortality difference challenges the routine adoption of empirical tuberculosis treatment in this setting, though the high proportion of infants requiring tuberculosis treatment in the standard-care group suggests clinical and diagnostic approaches identified tuberculosis risk effectively. These findings may inform guideline discussions about the optimal diagnostic strategy and timing of tuberculosis treatment initiation in severely ill, immunocompromised infants.
articles.evidence: Randomized controlled trial with 2×2 factorial design and group-sequential analysis across 19 hospitals in six countries (Côte d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe). Enrollment: 563 participants; 558 analysed (276 in empirical TB treatment groups, 282 in non-empirical groups). Loss to follow-up: 6% in empirical TB group, 7% in non-empirical group. Major limitations: open-label design (unblinded) may introduce bias in clinical decision-making; high crossover in the comparison group (46% eventually received tuberculosis treatment) substantially diminishes the contrast between strategies; missing data addressed by imputation, but the magnitude of missing data at key timepoints is not fully specified. The abstract does not detail the microbiological diagnostic performance or sensitivity of the testing modalities used.

articles.title: Chin Tuck Against Resistance Exercise With Feedback to Improve Swallowing, Eating, and Drinking in Frail Older People Admitted to Hospital With Pneumonia (CTAR-SwiFt): Randomized Controlled Feasibility Study.
articles.dek: A feasibility study of a feedback-enabled chin tuck exercise intervention (CTAR-SwiFt) in hospitalized older adults with pneumonia found that participants could perform the exercises, with modest improvements in swallowing measures, though recruitment and retention challenges were identified.
summary: CTAR-SwiFt is a novel rehabilitation intervention consisting of a feedback-enabled exercise ball squeezed under the chin with real-time mobile app feedback, designed to target anterior neck muscles involved in swallowing. This randomized controlled feasibility study enrolled 24 participants aged ≥75 years admitted to two UK hospitals with pneumonia; 21 were randomized to standard care (control), low-intensity (once daily), or high-intensity (twice daily) exercises over 12 weeks with 24-week follow-up.

Among those randomized, 52% (11/21) completed the study. The recruitment rate was 0.91 participants per month. Of those approached, 32% agreed to participate. Participants showed improvements in the Eating Assessment Tool-10 and 4 Question Test (swallowing screening measures), minimal change in the Functional Oral Intake Scale, and quality-of-life improvement on the EQ-5D-3L. Mean maximum chin tuck strength increased by 0.8 kgf. The low-intensity intervention demonstrated the best improvement. Medical complications and hospital readmission were the primary reasons for study withdrawal.

These feasibility results demonstrate that hospitalized frail older adults can perform CTAR exercises and tolerate the intervention device. However, the study was designed to assess usability and recruitment feasibility rather than to establish clinical efficacy. The authors recommend future investigation in community-dwelling older adults after pneumonia, as this population differs from the hospital-admitted cohort studied here.
articles.why: Swallowing difficulties in older people with pneumonia can affect nutrition, oral intake, and recovery. This study explores whether a structured, technology-enabled exercise intervention is acceptable and feasible in this vulnerable population, which could inform design of future efficacy trials. The finding that low-intensity exercise performed better than high-intensity suggests that intervention intensity may need careful calibration for frail hospitalized patients.
articles.evidence: Randomized controlled feasibility trial with 24 participants recruited and 21 randomized across three arms. Major limitations: small sample size reflecting feasibility scope; 52% completion rate with medical complications as primary withdrawal reason; lack of clinically meaningful effect sizes for most outcomes; study conducted in acute hospital setting, limiting generalizability to community-dwelling older adults; no information provided regarding blinding, baseline comparability of randomized groups, or statistical analysis plan. Uncertainty remains about whether findings apply to less acute populations and whether improvements in swallowing measures translate to clinically important functional changes.

articles.title: Economic Evaluations of Algorithm-Enabled Remote Monitoring of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices: Systematic Review.
articles.dek: A systematic review of economic evaluations for algorithm-enabled remote monitoring of cardiac devices finds potential value in some settings but heterogeneous evidence that limits direct comparison across studies.
summary: This systematic review identified 10 full economic evaluations of algorithm-enabled remote monitoring linked to cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) in adults with established or at-risk heart failure. Studies used models, trial data, or observational data and were sometimes embedded within health technology assessments. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across population definitions, intervention characteristics, algorithm types, monitored parameters, and economic methods.

Cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses were the predominant economic approaches, with time horizons ranging from short-term follow-up to lifetime modeling. Several studies reported economically favorable findings, including dominance (lower cost with better outcomes) or cost-effectiveness thresholds met. However, outcomes varied considerably, and favorable estimates typically depended on assumptions about reduced hospitalization and shorter hospital stays, whereas quality-adjusted life year gains were generally modest.

The reviewers conclude there is economic evidence suggesting potential value for algorithm-enabled CIED remote monitoring in some settings, but the methodological heterogeneity and variation in intervention design, modeling approaches, and clinical data limit certainty and applicability. The reporting of key implementation factors such as alert burden and diagnostic performance was limited. More robust, standardized evidence across different devices, algorithms, and health care settings is needed before economic conclusions can be applied confidently in practice.
articles.why: This review is clinically relevant because CIEDs with remote monitoring are increasingly deployed to detect early signs of deterioration, yet decision-makers face uncertainty about their economic value across different settings. The heterogeneity identified highlights why a single cost-effectiveness estimate from one study may not transfer to another institution or population. Understanding the range and drivers of economic outcomes—especially the reliance on hospitalization assumptions and modest quality-of-life gains—can inform discussions between clinicians, patients, and health systems about which remote monitoring approaches may deliver value in their specific contexts.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and health technology assessment sources. Included studies: 10 full economic evaluations using models, trial data, or observational data. Quality assessment: CHEQUE checklist and CHEERS 2022 statement. Data synthesis: Narrative due to heterogeneity. Limitations: One reviewer performed primary screening and data extraction with a second reviewer independently checking subsets; sample sizes of individual studies not reported in the abstract; substantial heterogeneity in intervention design, algorithm types, and economic methods limits meta-analysis; favorable cost-effectiveness estimates are sensitive to unvalidated assumptions about hospitalization reduction; diagnostic performance and alert burden reporting is incomplete; direct comparison across studies is difficult; transferability of findings across different devices, algorithms, and health care settings remains uncertain.

articles.tag: CARDIOVASCULAR OUTCOMES, GLP-1 AGONISTS, TYPE 2 DIABETES, META-ANALYSIS
articles.title: GLP-1-based therapies for reduction of heart failure and cardiovascular outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.dek: A meta-analysis of 11 randomized controlled trials found that GLP-1-based therapies reduced cardiovascular mortality, heart failure hospitalization, and nonfatal cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from 11 randomized controlled trials involving 81,948 participants to evaluate the cardiovascular and heart failure effects of GLP-1-based therapies. The analysis examined five prespecified outcomes: cardiovascular mortality, hospitalization for heart failure, unstable angina hospitalization, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), and nonfatal stroke.

GLP-1-based therapy significantly reduced cardiovascular mortality (RR: 0.85), hospitalization for heart failure (RR: 0.90), nonfatal MI (RR: 0.87), and nonfatal stroke (RR: 0.88) compared with placebo. No statistically significant reduction was observed for unstable angina hospitalization. All included studies were rated at low risk of bias, though the analysis noted variable heterogeneity across outcomes, with moderate heterogeneity for nonfatal MI and substantial heterogeneity for unstable angina.

The findings indicate consistent cardiovascular benefit from GLP-1-based therapies beyond glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk. The observed reductions in mortality and major adverse events support the broader clinical value of this drug class, though the authors note variability in treatment effects across individual studies warrants consideration.
articles.why: These results may inform clinical discussions about the role of GLP-1-based therapies in cardiovascular risk reduction for diabetic patients, particularly those with existing heart disease or high cardiovascular risk. The consistent reduction in mortality and hospitalization outcomes suggests potential benefits that extend beyond glucose management. However, the lack of significant benefit for unstable angina and variable effects across studies suggest that individual patient characteristics may influence outcomes.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Sample size: 11 trials, 81,948 total participants. Major limitations: Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed, particularly for nonfatal MI (I²=56%) and unstable angina (I²=83%), indicating variability in reported treatment effects. The abstract does not indicate whether the included trials specifically enrolled patients with and without diabetes or other population characteristics. The full methodology and individual trial characteristics are not available from this abstract.

articles.tag: GESTATIONAL HYPERTENSION; VASCULAR IMAGING; PREGNANCY CARDIOVASCULAR RISK
articles.title: Non-invasive vascular assessment in gestational hypertension and preeclampsia during pregnancy and the postpartum period: a systematic review.
articles.dek: A systematic review of 49 studies found that non-invasive vascular imaging can detect structural and functional abnormalities in blood vessels during and after pregnancies complicated by gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, though long-term clinical utility remains unclear.
summary: This systematic review synthesized evidence from 49 studies involving 32,683 participants that used non-invasive vascular assessment techniques during pregnancy and the postpartum period. The reviewed techniques included pulse-wave velocity (arterial stiffness), carotid intima-media thickness (vessel wall structure), flow-mediated dilation (endothelial function), ophthalmic artery Doppler (small vessel blood flow), and retinal imaging. The search covered major databases through May 2024, and findings were synthesized narratively due to heterogeneity in study design.

Women with gestational hypertension showed consistent patterns of abnormal vascular findings during pregnancy and postpartum: increased arterial stiffness (elevated pulse wave velocity and augmentation index), reduced endothelial function (decreased flow-mediated dilation), and thickened vessel walls (increased intima-media thickness). Ophthalmic artery Doppler and retinal imaging revealed variable changes in blood flow patterns and retinal vessel diameter. Notably, some of these abnormalities persisted from weeks to years after delivery, with retinal changes documented up to six years postpartum, though persistence was not uniformly reported across studies.

The authors conclude that non-invasive vascular assessments can identify both large and small vessel abnormalities and endothelial dysfunction in women with hypertensive pregnancies. However, they found insufficient evidence to recommend these tests as independent predictors of future cardiovascular events. The review highlights a gap between the ability to detect vascular abnormalities and their prognostic value, noting that standardized, prospective longitudinal studies are needed to establish clinical utility.
articles.why: Women with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia are known to have increased long-term cardiovascular risk. This review examines whether currently available non-invasive vascular imaging tools could identify women at highest risk for future heart disease and stroke. Such information could potentially inform postpartum follow-up strategies and early preventive interventions, though the evidence base is not yet robust enough to guide clinical decisions. The persistence of some vascular changes years after delivery suggests potential lasting effects on vascular health that warrant further investigation.
articles.evidence: Systematic review synthesizing narrative evidence from 49 observational studies with a combined population of 32,683 participants. Major limitations include substantial heterogeneity in study designs, measurement techniques, and reporting standards across included studies, which precluded meta-analysis. The abstract does not report effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical comparisons. The persistence of vascular abnormalities was described as 'inconsistent' across studies. The authors note that evidence remains insufficient to determine prognostic value or clinical application, indicating significant uncertainty about the predictive ability of these measurements for future cardiovascular events.

articles.title: Ketogenic Diet Effects on Liver Health in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: A Systematic Review.
articles.dek: A systematic review found that ketogenic diets were associated with improvements in liver fat, body weight, and metabolic markers in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, but evidence on fibrosis progression remains limited.
summary: This systematic review (following PRISMA guidelines) examined 14 studies—5 randomized controlled trials and 9 prospective cohort studies—involving 776 adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) or hepatic steatosis. Researchers compared ketogenic diet interventions against no dietary intervention or control diets, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through June 2026.

Ketogenic diet was associated with reductions in liver fat (ranging from −4.77% to 77% depending on measurement method), body weight loss (up to −12.0 kg), waist circumference reduction (up to −9.6 cm), and improvements in liver enzyme levels, lipid profiles, and glycemic markers. Prospective studies similarly showed decreases in controlled attenuation parameter, intrahepatic triglyceride, and Fatty Liver Index scores.

The authors concluded that ketogenic diet may improve disease severity indices, hepatic steatosis, and metabolic parameters in MASLD, but acknowledged that heterogeneity across studies prevented meta-analysis, and evidence regarding liver stiffness and fibrosis outcomes was limited and inconsistent. The authors called for larger, longer, and more standardized randomized trials.
articles.why: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is the most common chronic liver condition globally and is linked to lifestyle factors. This review synthesizes current evidence on ketogenic diet—an increasingly popular nutritional strategy—as a potential management tool. The findings may inform clinician discussions with patients about dietary options, though the limited evidence on fibrosis progression means that long-term disease course remains unclear. The inconsistency in fibrosis-related outcomes suggests caution in generalizing benefits across all disease stages.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review of 5 RCTs and 9 prospective cohort studies (N=776). Major limitations include methodological heterogeneity that precluded meta-analysis, variation in outcome measurement methods (different imaging and biomarker approaches), heterogeneity in study populations and intervention protocols, and sparse evidence on fibrosis-related outcomes. The abstract does not report individual study quality scores or specify the duration of follow-up across studies. Publication bias assessment is not mentioned. The authors did not perform meta-analysis due to study heterogeneity, limiting formal quantitative synthesis. No information is provided on registration status or funding sources.

articles.tag: PORTOSYSTEMIC SHUNT, INSULIN METABOLISM, GLUCOSE HOMEOSTASIS
articles.title: Changes in Circulating Insulin and Glucose Homeostasis After Portosystemic Shunt Creation and Obliteration: A Systematic Review.
articles.dek: A systematic review finds that portosystemic shunt creation raises circulating insulin by nearly 50% without changing fasting glucose, likely through reduced hepatic insulin clearance rather than increased secretion.
summary: This systematic review synthesized paired glucose and insulin measurements from 15 cohorts (17 records) before and after either transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) creation or endovascular shunt obliteration. The analysis pooled post-intervention to pre-intervention ratios using random-effects modeling with Hartung-Knapp adjustment, excluding studies at critical risk of bias.

After TIPS creation, fasting insulin increased by 49% (95% CI 24–80%), and the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance rose 55% (5–129%). By contrast, fasting glucose, glycated hemoglobin, and fructosamine remained unchanged. Glucose tolerance worsened in one of two tested cohorts. Insulin rose more prominently than C-peptide or proinsulin across four cohorts, and directly measured insulin sensitivity (by clamp) was unchanged. After shunt obliteration, fasting insulin fell 15% and insulin area-under-curve fell 17–19%.

The findings suggest that shunt creation impairs hepatic first-pass insulin extraction rather than increasing pancreatic secretion. The authors note that insulin-based resistance indices may be misleading after shunting and highlight the need for prospective studies on the long-term clinical consequences of shunt-induced hyperinsulinemia.
articles.why: Understanding how portosystemic shunts alter insulin and glucose homeostasis is relevant for clinicians managing patients with portal hypertension who undergo TIPS or shunt reversal. The discordance between raised insulin and unchanged fasting glucose suggests that standard glucose-based assessments may not capture metabolic changes after shunting. The findings could inform discussions about metabolic monitoring and risk stratification in this population, though no direct practice change is indicated from this evidence synthesis alone.
articles.evidence: Systematic review of observational cohort studies with paired measurements. Sample sizes per cohort were not uniformly reported in the abstract. Major limitations include heterogeneity in measurement timing and methods, variable study quality (critical bias risk excluded), and small numbers of cohorts contributing to some outcomes (e.g., 1–2 cohorts for obliteration effects). The abstract does not specify whether studies were randomized or observational, though the design implies observational data. Full methodological detail and risk-of-bias assessment are not provided in the abstract.

articles.tag: SGLT2 INHIBITORS; ELECTROLYTES; BONE METABOLISM; MASLD
articles.title: Dynamic trajectories of electrolytes and bone metabolism with tofogliflozin and glimepiride: A post-hoc analysis.
articles.dek: A 48-week randomized comparison of tofogliflozin and glimepiride in patients with type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease revealed that the SGLT2 inhibitor tofogliflozin modified serum electrolytes and bone turnover markers.
summary: This post-hoc analysis enrolled 40 participants with concurrent type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) who were randomly assigned to either tofogliflozin 20 mg daily or glimepiride 0.5–6.0 mg daily for 48 weeks. Researchers measured changes in anthropometric measures, serum and urinary electrolytes, and bone metabolism markers.

Tofogliflozin increased serum magnesium (from 2.0 to 2.13 mg/dL) and caused transient elevation of serum calcium and bone resorption marker tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5b. It transiently reduced serum potassium (from 4.05 to 3.89 mEq/L) and uric acid, with increased urinary potassium and uric acid excretion. Urinary magnesium and calcium excretion remained stable. In tofogliflozin-treated patients, improvements in liver histology (reduced steatosis and hepatocellular ballooning) correlated with increases in a bone turnover marker (type I collagen cross-linked N-telopeptide).

The findings suggest that SGLT2 inhibitors alter electrolyte handling and bone metabolism in patients with concurrent diabetes and fatty liver disease, with potential associations between hepatic improvement and bone remodeling. The clinical significance of transient electrolyte and bone marker changes remains to be determined.
articles.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly used in type 2 diabetes and MASLD. This study provides mechanistic observations about electrolyte and bone effects in this population, which may inform monitoring strategies and discussions about safety during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. The correlation between hepatic histological improvement and bone turnover markers raises questions about shared metabolic pathways that warrant further investigation.
articles.evidence: Randomized comparison with 40 total participants. Major limitations: post-hoc analysis (not prospectively registered or powered for specific hypotheses); small sample size; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values reported; comparison group (glimepiride) results not detailed in abstract; no information on loss to follow-up, adherence, or generalizability; duration is 48 weeks, limiting assessment of long-term effects or trajectory beyond study period.

articles.tag: DIETARY INFLAMMATORY INDEX · PEDIATRIC HYPERTENSION · META-ANALYSIS
articles.title: Association between dietary inflammatory index and high blood pressure in children: a meta-analysis.
articles.dek: A meta-analysis of six cross-sectional studies found that higher dietary inflammatory index scores were associated with increased odds of high blood pressure in children, though the evidence remains limited by study design and heterogeneity.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled data from six cross-sectional studies comprising 56,741 participants (nine independent datasets) of individuals under 18 years old. The researchers searched five databases through June 2026 and examined whether higher dietary inflammatory index (DII) scores—a measure of how pro-inflammatory a diet is—correlated with high blood pressure in children and adolescents.

Higher DII was associated with increased odds of high blood pressure (OR: 1.33, 95% CI: 1.04–1.70; p = 0.02), indicating a 33% higher odds with higher dietary inflammatory scores. The analysis showed moderate heterogeneity across studies. Sensitivity analyses revealed the pooled estimate was sensitive to individual study exclusion, with odds ratios ranging from 1.23 to 1.46 depending on which studies were removed. Subgroup analyses found no significant differences by geographic region, age, sex, DII cutoff values, BMI adjustment, or study quality.

The authors concluded that higher DII may be associated with increased odds of high blood pressure in children, but acknowledged substantial limitations. Study quality emerged as a significant moderator in meta-regression, with weaker associations observed in higher-quality studies. The cross-sectional designs preclude inference of causality, and heterogeneous definitions of high blood pressure across studies limit confidence in the overall findings.
articles.why: Understanding dietary patterns and their relationship to blood pressure in childhood may inform discussions about early cardiovascular prevention. However, the cross-sectional nature means dietary inflammatory index and high blood pressure were measured at the same time point, preventing determination of cause and effect. Clinicians should recognize this as preliminary observational evidence rather than demonstration of a causal link, and should await longitudinal studies and mechanistic research before considering DII modification as a targeted intervention strategy.
articles.evidence: Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six cross-sectional studies. Sample: 56,741 participants across nine independent datasets, all under 18 years old. Major limitations: (1) All included studies were cross-sectional, precluding causal inference; (2) moderate heterogeneity (I² = 65%) across studies; (3) sensitivity of pooled estimates to individual study exclusion, with loss of statistical significance after removing certain studies; (4) heterogeneous definitions and measurement of high blood pressure across studies; (5) study quality identified as a significant moderator, with weaker associations in higher-quality studies. No information provided on trial registration or funding sources.
